title: Build a Line from Slope and One Point

scenes.title: Slope 3 through (2,5) — what equation is it?
scenes.narration: Suppose a line has slope three and passes through the point two comma five. How do we build its equation without guessing the y-intercept? Here is the idea: slope tells us how y changes when x changes, while the point tells us one exact location the line must pass through. One slope and one point pin down one unique nonvertical line.

scenes.title: Why point-slope form works
body: Compare any point (x,y) to the known point (x1,y1).
change in y = slope × change in x
scenes.narration: Point-slope form is not a formula to memorize blindly. It comes directly from the meaning of slope. From the known point x one, y one to any other point x, y on the same line, the vertical change is y minus y one and the horizontal change is x minus x one. Since slope equals vertical change divided by horizontal change, multiplying both sides by the horizontal change gives y minus y one equals m times x minus x one.

scenes.title: The sign trap students miss
body: Subtract the coordinate exactly as written
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up: the x-coordinate belongs inside the parentheses with x, and the y-coordinate belongs with y. Also, keep the subtraction signs before simplifying. If a coordinate is negative, subtracting that negative becomes addition. For our point two comma five, substitute y one equals five and x one equals two, giving y minus five equals three times x minus two.

scenes.title: Now simplify — but interpret every step
scenes.narration: Now distribute the three: y minus five equals three x minus six. Add five to both sides, so y equals three x minus one. Notice why the slope stayed three. We only rewrote the same line into slope-intercept form; we did not change its geometry. The negative one is the y-intercept that the given slope and point force the line to have.

scenes.title: Quick verification
scenes.narration: Check the known point. Substitute x equals two into y equals three x minus one: y equals six minus one, which is five, so the point two comma five really lies on the line. The big idea is simple: slope describes the rate of change, the known point anchors the line, and point-slope form packages those two facts into one equation. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT.
